en: A MAN OF GOD
[ACT I]
The Lemoynes' drawing room. Cold, commonplace furnishings. On the wall, Burnand's "Parables" and a reproduction of the Sistine Madonna.
[SCENE I]
OSMONDE, MÉGAL : (They are standing; Mégal has not taken off his overcoat.)
MÉGAL : I beg your pardon, Mademoiselle. I see you were still at table. Besides, I told the maid not to disturb you.

OSMONDE : Please, do sit down. (Mégal sits.) It doesn't matter in the least. On Sundays we have lunch very late. There are always people who need to speak to my father after the service. Besides, we were finished.
MÉGAL : If I understood correctly, you were kind enough to offer to take the children out for a while this afternoon... I wanted to make sure I wasn't taking advantage...
OSMONDE : Not in the least. For once, I have my afternoon free.
MÉGAL : I don't know how to thank you... especially since I was wondering what I would have done with the little ones today. The maid is out for the day, and I am going to Épinay.
OSMONDE : Madame Mégal?...
MÉGAL : No change. Besides, an illness like that... if one can call it an illness.
OSMONDE : Is she suffering?
MÉGAL : It is impossible to say. She complains continuously, but... the doctors assure me there is an enormous element of autosuggestion in it.
OSMONDE : Oh?
MÉGAL : And that is really the only trait that reminds me of what she used to be. Because otherwise, she isn't the same person... (Lower.) One can't even say she is a person anymore.
OSMONDE : I don't know if Suzanne told you, but she answered very well this morning in Sunday school.
MÉGAL : Well, so much the better.
OSMONDE : Besides, I am very pleased with Yvonne too.
MÉGAL : They are good little girls... And where are you going to take them this afternoon?
OSMONDE : Well, I don't really know yet.
MÉGAL : If by chance I didn't return too late from Épinay, we could do as we did a fortnight ago...
OSMONDE (evasive) : We shall see; we'll trust to inspiration.
MÉGAL (looking at her) : That scarf is pretty; it suits you very well. (A silence.)
[SCENE II]
THE SAME, EDMÉE, CLAUDE, Mme LEMOYNE

EDMÉE (to Mégal, who has stood up) : Please, Monsieur, don't get up... (To Mme Lemoyne.) Mother, let me introduce Monsieur Mégal, who lives upstairs from us. Monsieur Mégal is the father of the little girls you met yesterday on the stairs.
Mme LEMOYNE : A pleasure, Monsieur...
CLAUDE : Won't you have a cup of coffee?

MÉGAL (standing) : Thank you, but I must go out to the suburbs. I was just telling Mademoiselle Osmonde how grateful I am to her for all she does for my little girls. She came again the other evening to hear their lessons; in a little while, she has kindly offered to take them for a walk...
EDMÉE (curtly) : But Monsieur, so long as she has the time, nothing could be more natural.
MÉGAL : I don't agree. Please don't trouble yourselves. Good afternoon, Monsieur... Madame... Mademoiselle... (He bows to Mme Lemoyne and exits.)
[SCENE III]
THE SAME, without MÉGAL
Mme LEMOYNE : That gentleman seems very nice.
EDMÉE : We don't know him at all.
Mme LEMOYNE : An open look in his eyes... a great deal of kindness in the mouth...
OSMONDE : A little coffee, Grandmother?
Mme LEMOYNE : Just a drop, darling... Your Uncle Francis would scold me. There, that's enough, enough.
CLAUDE : Why didn't Francis come to lunch with you, after all?
Mme LEMOYNE : He had a patient to see on the outskirts of Paris. In any case, he is coming to fetch me. (Lowering her voice.) I believe he has a word to say to you.
EDMÉE : What?
Mme LEMOYNE : I said he is coming to fetch me.
EDMÉE : You know we never see him. (To Claude.) Your brother hasn't visited more than two or three times since the holidays.

Mme LEMOYNE : You must admit, he is so terribly busy... I see it clearly now that I am here... The hospital, home visits, appointments, papers for the Academy... I wonder how he holds up. (To Claude.) But then, it's just the same with you, my dear boy; oh, I would never reproach you for doing your full duty, and more than your duty, as your dear father used to say. But this parish strikes me as very, very heavy. And with all that, do you get enough exercise? You see to that, don't you, Edmée?
EDMÉE : We are all in excellent health.
Mme LEMOYNE : This Parisian life is already so exhausting in itself... compared to Lausanne. Your coffee is delicious; you must give me the details for Francis.

EDMÉE : I'm sorry I can't help you. It probably comes from the grocer across the street. Will you excuse me, Mother? I must find a reading for my Young Women's Guild. (She kneels before a low bookcase.)
Mme LEMOYNE : But to return to that gentleman, do you look after those two sweet little girls regularly, Osmonde? That is so kind of you!
OSMONDE : I spend a little time with them now and then.
Mme LEMOYNE : And their mother?...
EDMÉE (leafing through a book) : Their mother is in an asylum.
Mme LEMOYNE : How dreadful!
EDMÉE (to Osmonde) : I'm rather surprised you have the afternoon free. Christmas falls a fortnight from Wednesday, and it seems to me you still have a great deal to do between now and then.
OSMONDE : Quite the contrary, I am ahead of schedule this year.
EDMÉE : Your needlework for your godmother is barely begun.

Mme LEMOYNE : It saddens me to think I won't see your Christmas tree. But Henri and Loulette are counting on me. It would be a terrible heartbreak if I weren't there for the holidays. It's so hard to please everyone... The misfortune of families that are too close.
EDMÉE (to Osmonde) : Do you remember The Little Orphan of the Priory?
OSMONDE : Let me see. (Edmée continues leafing through the book.)
Mme LEMOYNE : I remember it; it is utterly delightful. Besides, all those books adapted from the English are charming.
EDMÉE (putting down the book) : It strikes me as appallingly sentimental, and those girls are already only too inclined to weep over trifles.
CLAUDE : The important thing is to interest them.
EDMÉE : Not at any price.
Mme LEMOYNE : A little touch of romance does no harm... Just a tiny bit. (To Osmonde.) What do you think, darling?
OSMONDE (who has stood up) : I have no opinion.
EDMÉE : You haven't forgotten that Mademoiselle Gentil is expecting you at five o'clock to read to her.
OSMONDE (irritated) : Don't worry.
EDMÉE : It's all very well to take on new obligations...
OSMONDE : Goodbye, Grandmother. What are you doing this afternoon, Father?
CLAUDE : I have one or two letters to write. And my address for tomorrow to prepare.
EDMÉE : Little Simonin?
Mme LEMOYNE : I'm sure you never forget anything, Edmée, it's wonderful!
OSMONDE (bitterly) : No, Mother never forgets anything; Mother is terrible. (She exits.)
[SCENE IV]
THE SAME, without OSMONDE
Mme LEMOYNE : The dear girl is a little high-strung.
CLAUDE (to his wife) : Perhaps she doesn't feel trusted enough.
EDMÉE : I'd ask for nothing better. But despite her quiet ways, Osmonde is impulsive—I see it every day.
CLAUDE : I wonder whether by constantly noting someone's faults, one doesn't exaggerate them, so to speak. Don't you think so, Mother?
EDMÉE : So one should just close one's eyes?
CLAUDE : I'm not saying that, but the way we treat others...
EDMÉE : I know the theory, but it can lead rather far...
Mme LEMOYNE : At any rate, I am delighted with my granddaughter... You know, they are organizing lectures in Lausanne now during the summer semester, excursions, and...
CLAUDE : I see what you're leading up to.
Mme LEMOYNE : Naturally.
CLAUDE : But I have no desire to lend you my daughter.

EDMÉE : We'll talk about that later. (To Claude.) Well, what are you answering Monsieur Junod? (To Mme Lemoyne.) The pastor of La Chaux-de-Fonds asked us to recommend lodgings for his son, who is coming to prepare for his degree. You know, Fred.
CLAUDE : If you think we can decently offer him the small bedroom...
EDMÉE : A young man ought to be able to make do with it, don't you think, Mother?
Mme LEMOYNE : Why, I would have been quite content with it if Francis hadn't insisted that I stay at his place. Besides, I am wonderfully looked after.
CLAUDE : Then I shall write to him along those lines. (He exits.)
[SCENE V]
Mme LEMOYNE : But Fred is a very young man; aren't you afraid that Osmonde...
EDMÉE : He's a simpleton. I don't think Osmonde has much taste for that sort. No, that isn't what I would fear for her.
Mme LEMOYNE : Do you mean you have other fears? ...seems to have shaken you at the time. No? A secret, no doubt? That did not belong to him... (Evasive gesture from Mme Lemoyne.)
Mme LEMOYNE : Only, of course, if you have this anxiety...
EDMÉE (after giving her an inquiring look) : Ah, well, you are speaking of Osmonde now... I wasn't following. Anxiety is saying too much. I am wary, that is all.
Mme LEMOYNE : Yet it seems to me she takes so much after her father...
EDMÉE : You think so?
Mme LEMOYNE : In character, at any rate...
EDMÉE (in an ambiguous tone) : Yes, yes...
Mme LEMOYNE : As my poor husband used to say: "it is the same ring of the soul."
EDMÉE : I have not yet had the privilege of hearing my daughter's soul.
Mme LEMOYNE : But Claude, if he shared your concerns, would surely have...
EDMÉE : Claude tells you everything?
Mme LEMOYNE : Everything he has the right to tell me.
EDMÉE : In any case, when I see the little volume he sends you every week...

Mme LEMOYNE : I could never say enough how much good that correspondence has done me. I recently reread some of Claude's old letters; there are some that are so beautiful, so poignant, that I almost copied out passages for you.
EDMÉE : When were those letters written?
Mme LEMOYNE : From the early years of your marriage.
EDMÉE : And you say they are poignant?
Mme LEMOYNE : At that time Claude went through a very painful crisis of conscience. You know very well that for a moment he even thought of giving up his ministry.
EDMÉE : What?
Mme LEMOYNE : You're not going to make me believe that you suspected nothing.

EDMÉE : Nothing at all. The early days of our married life were... we weren't precisely intimate then. But I ask you once more to tell me exactly when those letters date from. Are they prior... to nineteen hundred and three, for example?
Mme LEMOYNE : They are all prior to nineteen hundred and three. Why that question?
EDMÉE : Mother, there is no need to pretend, I assure you. Just now, you already... hush!
[SCENE VI]
THE SAME, CLAUDE
CLAUDE : Do you remember the Junods' address? I can't put my hand on his letter anymore. Is it still Rue Karl-Marx?
EDMÉE : I believe they moved; don't you remember, Mother?

Mme LEMOYNE : I have not kept in touch with them. They have become completely Bolshevik, like everyone in La Chaux-de-Fonds, for that matter. Your father, who had so much common sense, was already alarmed by it.
EDMÉE : It's astonishing that you can't find that letter; I put it this morning in the pigeonhole for unanswered mail.
CLAUDE : Ah, right!...
EDMÉE : Really, Claude, I've told you once and for all... do have some order in this house!
CLAUDE : Order to that degree drives me mad. Well, I'll finish up and be right back. (He exits.)
[SCENE VII]
EDMÉE : So, this crisis of conscience... Come now, Claude is not a man to have ever known certain agonies. Everything is so clear to him, so simple. Thank God! What would have become of me otherwise?
Mme LEMOYNE : We all owe him a great debt, that is certain.
EDMÉE : Oh! But it isn't gratitude I am talking about at all. One doesn't thank someone for being who he is. (With deep intensity.) So you are sure it was before nineteen hundred and three?
Mme LEMOYNE : After that time, on the contrary, it's as if a calm descended; one would say he saw a light he had never perceived before.
EDMÉE : A light?
Mme LEMOYNE : Yes, the kind that only shows itself when it is completely dark. (A silence.) Why are you laughing?
EDMÉE (dully) : Ah! How fine promises are!
Mme LEMOYNE : What promises?
EDMÉE : He promised me that you would never know anything.
Mme LEMOYNE : But really, Edmée...
EDMÉE : Oh, there's no use trying to deceive me anymore... That secret... our secret... he has... the wretch!..
Mme LEMOYNE : Him, a wretch! You dare insult him!
[SCENE VIII]
THE SAME, CLAUDE, a letter in his hand
CLAUDE : My letter is finished. If you go out, you can post it.

EDMÉE : It's Sunday. I don't think there will be another collection. Besides, a day won't matter. Or else... You can give it to me all the same... What time is it? (A frantic gesture betrays her inner turmoil.)
CLAUDE : But what is the matter with you, Edmée?
EDMÉE : Nothing... nothing at all.
CLAUDE : Mother...
EDMÉE : Will you still be here when I return?
CLAUDE : It seems Francis is coming. I'll wait for him.
EDMÉE : Yes, but you... you... I won't be long. (Lower.) I want to find you alone, do you understand? Over there I'll manage; there will surely be someone to take my place.
Mme LEMOYNE : As for me, Edmée, I shall be gone by the time you return.
EDMÉE : Goodbye, Mother. (She exits.)
[SCENE IX]
CLAUDE : What is going on?

Mme LEMOYNE : My poor child, I was indiscreet. I don't know how I was led into it... (She is on the verge of tears.) Deep down, the wonder is that it didn't happen much sooner. Edmée has just discovered that you told me everything. (A silence.)

CLAUDE (forcefully) : So much the better... You see, Mother, that lie towards her weighed on me terribly; how many times have I not reproached myself for it! If I hadn't had some vague apprehension, I would have confessed it to her years ago...
Mme LEMOYNE : What a word to use!
CLAUDE : I had pledged not to tell you anything.
Mme LEMOYNE : Because she had demanded it. But by what right did she make such a demand?
CLAUDE : No matter; I had promised.
Mme LEMOYNE : But remember: she was threatening to leave, perhaps even to... Well! The promises one makes to an invalid!...

CLAUDE : In any case, ever since Edmée regained her health, ever since I cured her, I ought to have told her everything; she would have understood. You yourself always say one must have trust. Besides, when I made that promise, I intended to keep it. And then, one day... I don't know why... I didn't feel any more alone than usual: I wrote it all to you.
Mme LEMOYNE : You have no need to apologize.
CLAUDE : I treated her like a child.
Mme LEMOYNE : And after all, Claude, after all this time...
CLAUDE : The look in her eyes just now when she went out, oh! I recognized it only too well... Mother, everything I had so painfully won, I may have just lost.
Mme LEMOYNE : Through my fault.
CLAUDE : No. I alone am guilty. In a little while, I shall ask her to forgive me.
Mme LEMOYNE : You would humble yourself like that before the woman who... As for me, I know very well that I could never forgive her.
CLAUDE : Forgiveness, Mother, has meaning only between her and me.
Mme LEMOYNE : She didn't deserve someone like you.

CLAUDE : When I think of all that forgiveness brought to me... of that inner peace... that sense of a strength willing alongside you, but not in your place... It was truly from that day on that the world was illuminated for me. Before, I was groping in the dark... The ordeal, Mother. Before those terrible months, that word seemed hollow to me. But when one has lived through what I lived through...
Mme LEMOYNE : She suspected so little of it!

CLAUDE : The finest part of the ordeal was precisely that she did not understand. I was all alone... with Him. And then, little by little, when I felt her regaining confidence... The way she would look at me at times when she thought I wasn't paying attention! That silent appeal in her eyes! It was as though I were helping something to live... something so fragile... something that had every reason to die. In the early days, when I came home in the evening, why, I was always expecting to learn that she had left to join him! I am certain that for a very long time she still thought of it... she believed she was thinking of it. But in reality, between her and him there was a force. And then one day I suddenly had the certainty that it was over—that she no longer thought of it—that we had won. You must not weep, Mother. I shouldn't have stirred up all these memories...
Mme LEMOYNE : She is going to hurt you again.

CLAUDE : That was possible in the past, in the days when we had not yet suffered. But now, we no longer could. Each has also borne the other's cross; each has bled for the other. We are as if enriched—better, yes, better...
Mme LEMOYNE : Ah! You express all that so well! (She wipes her eyes.)
CLAUDE : The bell just rang twice. That must be Francis. Will you excuse me? The maid is out; I have to answer the door myself. (He exits.)
Mme LEMOYNE (alone, to herself) : Too good, too generous. (She shakes her head sorrowfully.)
[SCENE X]
THE SAME, FRANCIS
CLAUDE : My dear fellow, you should have come to lunch.
FRANCIS : I had a patient to see in Jouy-en-Josas; I didn't get back until two o'clock.
Mme LEMOYNE : When did you have lunch?

FRANCIS : Half an hour ago, at an automat. (To Claude.) So, how are things? I just saw someone from the consistory who spoke to me about you. I say, they really seem to hold you in high esteem! Word has it you've galvanized the parish, that the members of your church swear by you.
Mme LEMOYNE : Why do you never come to hear him?
FRANCIS : What do you expect? It's not my line. (To Claude.) Did Mother warn you that I have a word to say to you?
CLAUDE : Yes, but I have no idea what it's about.
FRANCIS : Look, Mother, as I told you... naturally you may stay; but you know I am going to have to touch upon a rather painful subject with Claude. I wouldn't want to upset you unnecessarily.
Mme LEMOYNE : If I am not in the way, I would prefer...
FRANCIS : It concerns... Michel Sandier.
CLAUDE : Ah! (Movement from Mme Lemoyne.)
FRANCIS : Michel Sandier came to consult me recently.
Mme LEMOYNE : That is unheard of.

FRANCIS : There is nothing extraordinary in that; he knows through medical journals, which it seems he reads diligently, that my research deals precisely with the very grave condition from which he is currently suffering.
CLAUDE : So, it is a condition...?
FRANCIS (in a low voice) : Yes. Incurable as things stand. (Aloud.) Besides, he had another reason for insisting on seeing me, in particular.
Mme LEMOYNE : Ah!
FRANCIS : Mother, you can see that Claude is keeping his composure.
Mme LEMOYNE : He has too much. As for me, the mere name of that wretch...
FRANCIS : Michel Sandier has only a short time left to live, and he knows he is doomed. I must even say that he contemplates his situation with a lucidity and a calmness that struck me.
Mme LEMOYNE : Probably some sort of pose.
CLAUDE : Mother!
FRANCIS : For years he has led a life upon which I didn't ask him to dwell, but which naturally is not unrelated to his present condition.
CLAUDE : And then?
